stories.headline: Polis requests federal disaster declaration for Colorado wildfires amid growing tensions with White House
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis has submitted a formal 50-page request to the federal government for a major disaster declaration following this summer's Colorado wildfires, which would unlock FEMA assistance for affected communities. The declaration would benefit Pueblo, Custer and Ouray counties, helping rebuild roads, water treatment plants, parks and other public infrastructure damaged or destroyed by the blazes. Federal aid would also be available to uninsured homeowners, a critical issue in communities like Beulah where multiple residents say they were denied insurance coverage due to wildfire risk.

Presidential approval for such requests is typically routine, but Colorado faces a difficult political environment. Trump denied the state's request for federal disaster assistance following the 2025 Elk and Lee fires and subsequent flooding on the Western Slope — the first denial Colorado had received in 35 years. The state appealed that denial and was turned down again.

Polis framed the new request as one that meets all legal requirements, noting that flooding and debris flows on burn scars have compounded destruction and claimed at least one life. 'These disasters clearly meet all the requirements for a major disaster declaration,' Polis said in a news release. The governor said Colorado has committed significant state resources but that the scale of the disaster requires a federal partnership for full recovery.

By comparison, President Biden approved federal aid for the 2021 Marshall Fire within hours of Colorado's request, and President Obama acted within days following the catastrophic 2013 Front Range floods. State emergency management officials say rural electric cooperatives would also qualify for assistance in rebuilding lost power lines and transmission infrastructure.

stories.headline: William Hood named Colorado Supreme Court's next chief justice
stories.summary:
The Colorado Supreme Court has selected Justice William Hood to serve as the court's next chief justice, succeeding Chief Justice Monica Márquez, whose term expires in August 2027. Hood has been a member of the court since 2014 and will undergo a one-year onboarding period mentoring under Márquez before formally assuming the role.

Before joining the Supreme Court, Hood spent seven years as a judge on the Denver District Court and previously served as a litigation partner at Isaacson Rosenbaum P.C. in Denver. He also spent a decade as a prosecutor in Colorado's 18th Judicial District.

'Justice Hood brings deep experience, steady judgment, and a genuine commitment to the people we serve,' Márquez said in a news release. Hood said he was honored by the confidence his colleagues placed in him and expressed gratitude for Márquez's willingness to guide him through the transition.

The chief justice position carries a three-year rotating term. The appointment represents a significant leadership transition at the state's highest court.

stories.headline: Tina Peters reported to have received job offer to help oversee elections in California county
stories.summary:
Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk convicted of election security breaches whose sentence was commuted by Gov. Jared Polis earlier this year, has reportedly been offered a position as assistant clerk and registrar in Shasta County, California, according to Colorado Sun columnist Mike Littwin. Shasta County Clerk Clint Curtis, himself an election denier who has already been voted out of office, announced the potential hire on a podcast affiliated with the Jefferson State secession movement.

The offer has already become mired in controversy. The position Curtis wants to give Peters is currently filled by Brent Turner, who is on sick leave for a serious illness and says he has no intention of resigning. Curtis, who has been censured by the county Board of Supervisors over personnel issues, told a radio station he estimates only a 70 percent chance the arrangement comes together.

The news has renewed scrutiny of Polis's decision to commute Peters' sentence over the unanimous objection of the state Clemency Board. A recently revealed 'smoking gun' email from a Trump administration aide showed White House pressure on cabinet officials to find ways to punish Colorado for resisting Trump's demand to free Peters, whom he described as a political prisoner. Polis has declined to discuss any conversations he may have had with White House officials regarding the commutation.

Peters herself, in a recent podcast appearance, credited White House counsel David Warrington for working 'with the administration, Polis,' for her release, adding another layer of questions about the circumstances surrounding the commutation.

stories.headline: Rockies set franchise record with ninth consecutive home loss at Coors Field, completing sweep by Guardians
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies have set a franchise record for their longest home losing streak at Coors Field, dropping nine straight games in LoDo after being swept by the Cleveland Guardians over the weekend. The Guardians closed out the sweep with a 7-2 victory Sunday, following a 9-1 loss Friday and a 4-3 defeat Saturday. The nine-game home skid matches the club's overall record set by the 1993 Rockies, who played at Mile High Stadium, and is the first time in franchise history Colorado has been swept in three consecutive home series.

The losing streak also stands as the longest home skid in all of Major League Baseball this season. During the nine-game stretch, the Rockies were outscored 70-37, their pitching staff posted a 6.96 ERA overall and starters recorded a 10.04 ERA. Colorado falls to 50-80 on the season, now 30 games under .500.

The Rockies need to go 13-20 over their final 33 games to avoid becoming the fifth franchise in MLB history to lose 100 or more games in four consecutive seasons. Colorado now departs on a seven-game road trip to Washington and Atlanta before returning to Coors Field on Aug. 31 against Baltimore.

The record-setting home loss came on an otherwise celebratory day at 20th and Blake. The Rockies unveiled a 15-foot bronze statue of Hall of Famer Larry Walker outside Coors Field before Sunday's game, honoring the franchise's most decorated position player. Walker was visibly emotional during the ceremony, attended by family, former teammates and hundreds of fans.

stories.headline: Avalanche GM Joe Sakic 'pretty confident' Cale Makar will sign extension before season starts
stories.summary:
Colorado Avalanche general manager Joe Sakic said Sunday he is confident that superstar defenseman Cale Makar will sign a contract extension before the 2026-27 season begins, though no deal is yet in place. Sakic made the remarks ahead of the second annual Avalanche-University of Denver alumni game at Magness Arena. 'I'm pretty confident that he'll be signed before the season starts. I'm not worried about it,' Sakic said.

Makar, a two-time Norris Trophy winner, is entering the final year of a six-year, $54 million contract. His next deal is expected to be the largest in franchise history and could be worth twice as much per season or more as the NHL salary cap has risen rapidly in recent years. A key CBA deadline looms: the maximum contract length under the current agreement is eight years for re-signing a player, and that window closes Sept. 15 when a new collective bargaining agreement takes effect.

Coach Jared Bednar and forward Artturi Lehkonen are also entering the final years of their contracts without extensions. Sakic expressed similar calm about both situations. Bednar is entering his 11th season as head coach, making him the second-longest tenured coach in the league behind Tampa Bay's Jon Cooper.

Lehkonen posted 21 goals and 48 points in 70 games last season before suffering an injury during the second round of the playoffs. Sakic indicated dialogue with all three parties has been positive and that he does not expect any of the situations to become disruptive heading into training camp.

stories.headline: Denver's Wyndham Clark wins BMW Championship for his third PGA Tour victory of 2026 season
stories.summary:
Colorado native and Valor Christian graduate Wyndham Clark won the BMW Championship at Bellerive Golf Course in St. Louis on Sunday, shooting a final-round 70 to finish 17-under par and claim his third PGA Tour title of the 2026 season. Clark birdied the final three holes to hold off Rory McIlroy, who bogeyed the 17th and made par on the 18th after the two were tied heading into the back stretch of the closing holes.

The 32-year-old Clark was shaky through his first 15 holes, making three bogeys with no birdies, but a clutch birdie putt on the par-3 16th shifted the momentum. He and McIlroy had been tied on the tee before Clark made his putt and McIlroy missed. Clark followed with birdies on 17 and 18 to secure the win.

'It shows I'm one of the best players in the world,' Clark said after the round. 'Three wins in one season is my best year yet, coming off my worst season.' The BMW Championship is a FedEx Cup playoff event, further bolstering Clark's case for PGA Tour Player of the Year honors alongside his 2026 U.S. Open win at Shinnecock Hills.

Clark now advances to the Tour Championship at East Lake, where the FedEx Cup title will be decided. Patrick Cantlay finished runner-up and also advanced to East Lake, while Colorado's Gary Woodland made the top 30 and returns to the Tour Championship for the first time since 2019 as he continues to recover from brain surgery three years ago.

stories.headline: Bear found in Denver's Platt Park neighborhood, tranquilized and relocated by wildlife officials
stories.summary:
A young male black bear was discovered Sunday morning in a tree near East Louisiana Avenue and South Pennsylvania Street in Denver's Platt Park neighborhood, according to Colorado Parks and Wildlife. The roughly 100-pound, 18-month-old bear was tranquilized by wildlife authorities, caught in a tarp and removed from the area. CPW spokesperson Kara Van Hoose said officials were uncertain how the bear made its way into Denver, as there had been no prior reports of bear activity in the area.

The bear has since been transported away from the city. 'He's on his way back to where bears should be — not Denver,' Van Hoose said. The incident is one of a rising number of bear encounters being reported across Colorado this year.

CPW reports that the state is on pace to record its highest number of bear reports since implementing a statewide digital reporting system in 2019, with nearly double the typical number of encounters logged so far this year. Wildlife officials attribute the increase to widespread drought conditions that have disrupted bears' normal food-gathering activities, pushing them into human-occupied areas in search of sustenance.

stories.headline: Colorado standardized test scores tell a complicated story about student learning, educators say
stories.summary:
Fewer than half of Colorado's third graders — just 40.8 percent — could read and write at grade level last year according to results from the Colorado Measures of Academic Success, the state's annual standardized test administered to students beginning in third grade. The figures come despite a 2012 state law prioritizing reading and writing and approximately $39 million in state spending this year alone on literacy initiatives including teacher training in the science of reading.

However, educators across Colorado are pushing back on a strict interpretation of the scores. Critics of CMAS point to four core concerns: that the test captures only a single point in time, that participation rates affect results, that the test may not reflect the full breadth of student learning, and that consequences tied to low scores — including state accreditation ratings — can distort how schools respond to the assessments.

'It's one point in time, one day,' said Lisa Yates, superintendent of the high-performing Buena Vista School District. 'It does give some information, but there's so much other information about a student's reading ability that may not be captured in that one moment in time.' Three Colorado school districts received the state's lowest 'turnaround' accreditation rating last year based heavily on CMAS performance.

The CMAS program costs the state $18.3 million and the federal government $2.2 million annually. Colorado Education Commissioner Susana Córdova has described the test as a 'measuring stick' to help state leaders, teachers and parents understand how students are performing relative to peers statewide. The debate mirrors national tensions over standardized testing and its role in educational accountability.

stories.headline: Youth travel sports industry costs Colorado families tens of thousands of dollars annually, fueled by fear of missing out
stories.summary:
Colorado families are spending anywhere from thousands to tens of thousands of dollars annually on youth travel sports, driven by a nationwide pay-to-play club model that has overtaken recreational leagues and left many parents wrestling with financial and emotional costs. The Aspen Institute estimates the youth sports industry generates more than $40 billion annually and is expected to reach $70 billion by 2030 as club organizations, training facilities and private coaching businesses continue to expand.

For Joe Amorosa of the Denver area, the price of supporting his 10-year-old son Vinny — a multiple-time youth state wrestling champion — runs approximately $10,000 per year in club fees and travel tournament costs. Amorosa says that figure is modest compared to some families in his own club. 'All of youth sports has become a fear-of-missing-out gig,' he said. 'If you win Tulsa Nationals, you should win Reno Tournament of Champions. You do well there, you should go to the Super 32. You can get to this black hole that you can't escape if you let it consume you.'

The pressure to join club teams at increasingly younger ages is felt across sports, not just in Colorado but nationally. Families cite concerns that skipping travel competition will leave their children behind developmentally, a dynamic that club organizations have been effective at reinforcing through marketing and culture.

Sports medicine professionals and child development experts have raised concerns about early specialization and burnout, while the financial barrier to high-level youth sports participation raises equity concerns about which children have access to competitive development pathways.

stories.headline: Denver police urge vehicle registration renewals ahead of regional enforcement campaign
stories.summary:
Denver police are urging residents with expired vehicle registrations to renew them before an upcoming regional enforcement campaign brings increased traffic stops and citations, according to Denver7. The campaign will result in officers actively pulling over drivers with out-of-date registration plates across the metro area.

Officials did not specify the exact start date of the enforcement push but indicated it is imminent. Residents can renew vehicle registrations online through the Colorado Division of Motor Vehicles or in person at county clerk offices. Fines for expired registration in Colorado can reach several hundred dollars depending on how long the registration has lapsed.

stories.headline: Stanley Marketplace marks 10th anniversary with three-day celebration in Aurora
stories.summary:
Stanley Marketplace in Aurora is marking its 10th anniversary with a three-day celebration, commemorating a decade since the repurposed Stanley Aviation building opened as one of the Denver metro area's most distinctive mixed-use retail and dining destinations. The milestone event is expected to draw large crowds to the complex, which houses dozens of locally owned businesses including restaurants, breweries, fitness studios and specialty shops.

The anniversary underscores Stanley Marketplace's emergence as a community anchor in the Aurora area since its 2016 opening. The adaptive reuse project converted the historic 1954 Stanley Aviation manufacturing facility into a bustling indoor-outdoor market that has become a model for community-centered commercial development in the metro region.

topStory.headline: US-Canada Trade War Deepens as 50% Tariffs Take Effect, Negotiations Collapse
topStory.summary:
Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada broke down Friday, and new American tariffs of 50 percent on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods — roughly 5.5 percent of Canada's annual exports to the United States — took effect Saturday. The levies cover more than 500 product categories including whisky, honey, agricultural products, clothing, furniture, cameras and sporting goods such as hockey sticks. Some goods previously shielded under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade pact negotiated during Trump's first term, are now subject to the new tariffs, raising broader questions about the USMCA's future.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said negotiations collapsed late Friday after the United States introduced conditions he described as "uneconomic, unfair" and damaging to Canadian sovereignty. Among the objectionable demands, Carney said, were restrictions on Canada's ability to negotiate independent trade agreements with other countries and language he characterized as threatening to Quebec's French-language culture. "In short, they asked too much, and they offered too little," Carney said Saturday in Ottawa. He announced that Canada would impose dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs beginning September 8, targeting American steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

President Trump defended the tariffs on his Truth Social platform, claiming Canada has long charged American farmers excessive tariffs and asserting that Canada "wants the benefits of being a State, without being one" — a reference to his repeated suggestions that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state. To impose the 50 percent levies, Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a provision of the Depression-era Smoot-Hawley legislation that authorizes the president to place import taxes of up to 50 percent on goods from countries deemed to have discriminated against American businesses. The provision has never previously been used to raise tariffs, requires no formal investigation to invoke, and carries no statutory time limit.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said no further talks are scheduled, and both governments appear to have set aside near-term prospects for a negotiated settlement. Canada sends approximately 72 percent of its goods exports to the United States, making the American market critical to its economy. Economists and trade attorneys warn that beyond the direct cost of the tariffs themselves, prolonged uncertainty over trade policy risks chilling cross-border investment, disrupting manufacturing supply chains, and complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to control inflation. "Nearly all industries and professions are likely to see downstream effects from this spiraling trade dispute," said Augustine Lo of the law firm Dorsey and Whitney.

Some U.S. lawmakers, including Democratic Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont, have criticized the tariffs as harmful to border-state businesses that depend on cross-border commerce. Others have suggested the standoff may follow a pattern seen elsewhere in the Trump administration's trade approach: aggressive brinkmanship followed eventually by a negotiated agreement. For now, however, no talks are scheduled, and both governments have signaled they are prepared to absorb further economic friction before returning to the table.
